highlights: # Top AI companies have discussed creating their own standards body. Anthropic, Google and OpenAI have discussed creating an AI industry standards body, people familiar with the situation told CNN. According to those familiar with the situation, the catalyst for the discussions was a July essay written by Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis, who proposed a US-led Standards Body modeled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. The conversations are ongoing, one of the people said, and they are continuing with or without the Trump administration. The White House has an opaque system in place where AI companies can voluntarily submit their latest models for government review up to 30 days before they are publicly released. House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday there’s little consensus among the companies, who are fierce competitors, on what the standards and guardrails should be.

Every major release from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google raises the same question: What happens if the feature you’ve spent the last year building suddenly becomes part of the platform? That changes almost every strategic decision — from what products to build and where to differentiate to how to raise capital and create lasting value. One of the biggest strategic risks facing AI startups today isn’t losing to another founder — it’s discovering that your competitive advantage has become someone else’s product update. This session explores where defensibility still exists, how founders can respond when AI giants move into adjacent markets, and what separates companies that become features from those that remain businesses. Rather than reacting to every new model release, founders will hear where defensibility still exists, what enterprise and startup buyers continue to value, and how to build companies that remain relevant as AI evolves. If you’re building an AI company, the question isn’t whether foundation models will continue to evolve.

Tether AI Research recently shared the open-source release of VisionPsy-Nano, a compact vision-language model (VLM) purpose-built for on-device and edge deployment that outperforms comparable models in its weight class, including Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-VL-450M and Hugging Face’s SmolVLM2-500M. A vision-language model is an AI system that pairs a text-processing language model with an image encoder, enabling it to perceive and reason about visual data. But for AI that runs directly on a smartphone, the real frontier sits at a much smaller scale: models of around half a billion parameters, small enough to fit within the memory and power budget of an everyday phone while still delivering dependable quality. This size class has become one of the most active fronts in open model development, with Liquid AI’s LFM vision models and Hugging Face’s SmolVLM and nanoVLM series as the closest peers at this scale.

highlights: ## Robi Axiata and Grameenphone join Bangladesh's AI subscription race. Bangladesh telcos Grameenphone and Robi Axiata have launched separate AI subscription services that aim to make overseas AI models easier to access and pay for. On Thursday, Grameenphone launched OneAI, which gives customers access to eight AI models, including ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek and Gemini. Grameenphone’s OneAI launch follows hot on the heels of Robi Axiata, which rolled out a similar service last Wednesday called Robi AI Space in partnership with Every.AI. Robi AI Space, accessible via the telco’s MyRobi app, brings AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek directly to local consumers, who can pay for them via a single subscription, or by purchasing AI tokens using local mobile data bundles. Robi’s MD and CEO Ziad Shatara said making AI models easier to pay for removes a key barrier to AI adoption in Bangladesh, as international AI models require credit card payments, while credit card penetration in Bangladesh currently sits at just 1.6%.

highlights: Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s global policy chief, told reporters on Tuesday that the company has been working with rivals Anthropic and Google DeepMind on AI safety for weeks, as first reported by Bloomberg. The revelation comes in the wake of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay, published Saturday, which called for the industry to work together to slow the pace of frontier AI and avoid catastrophic risks. AI leaders across the industry, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Google’s Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, supported Amodei’s letter and call to action, with Altman saying that OpenAI would join Anthropologic in embedding third party evaluators into the company to monitor for safety. week.title: Top AI companies have discussed creating their own standards body - CNN
week.summary: # Top AI companies have discussed creating their own standards body. Anthropic, Google and OpenAI have discussed creating an AI industry standards body, people familiar with the situation told CNN. Ac...
highlights: # Top AI companies have discussed creating their own standards body. Anthropic, Google and OpenAI have discussed creating an AI industry standards body, people familiar with the situation told CNN. According to those familiar with the situation, the catalyst for the discussions was a July essay written by Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis, who proposed a US-led Standards Body modeled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. The conversations are ongoing, one of the people said, and they are continuing with or without the Trump administration. The White House has an opaque system in place where AI companies can voluntarily submit their latest models for government review up to 30 days before they are publicly released. House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday there’s little consensus among the companies, who are fierce competitors, on what the standards and guardrails should be.

week.title: Learn how to build lasting AI defensibility at Disrupt 2026 - TechCrunch
week.summary: It may be the platform you’re building on. Every major release from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google raises the same question: What happens if the feature you’ve spent the last year building suddenly beco...
highlights: It may be the platform you’re building on. Every major release from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google raises the same question: What happens if the feature you’ve spent the last year building suddenly becomes part of the platform? That changes almost every strategic decision — from what products to build and where to differentiate to how to raise capital and create lasting value. One of the biggest strategic risks facing AI startups today isn’t losing to another founder — it’s discovering that your competitive advantage has become someone else’s product update. This session explores where defensibility still exists, how founders can respond when AI giants move into adjacent markets, and what separates companies that become features from those that remain businesses. Rather than reacting to every new model release, founders will hear where defensibility still exists, what enterprise and startup buyers continue to value, and how to build companies that remain relevant as AI evolves. If you’re building an AI company, the question isn’t whether foundation models will continue to evolve.
